chief_complaint: sudden severe shortness of breath, chest pain, and fever 3 days after returning from Nigeria
hpi_details: Presents to emergency department with a 24-hour history of rapidly worsening shortness of breath, sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain, high fever (38.8°C), and productive cough producing rusty-coloured sputum. Three days ago, she returned from a 3-week trip visiting family in rural Nigeria, where she stayed in crowded housing. Complains of chills, rigors, severe fatigue, and feeling completely washed out. Has a history of type 2 diabetes and takes metformin.
ideas: thinks she caught tropical malaria or severe flu while travelling in Africa
concerns: terrified she will collapse and require breathing machine intensive care
expectations: wants urgent malaria blood tests, IV fluids, and strong pneumonia antibiotics immediately
pmh: type 2 diabetes mellitus x6 years, hypertension
social_hx: never smoked, zero alcohol, school administration officer, recent international travel

investigation_events.title: Urgent pneumonia and travel-related results
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent pneumonia and malaria-screening results are now available; oxygen and empiric treatment should not be delayed when indicated.

results.value: Dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small right pleural effusion

results.test: Malaria rapid antigen and thick/thin films

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Community-Acquired Pneumonia is essential for appropriate diagnostic workup and treatment.
Clinical history, severity assessment, and targeted testing must be interpreted together rather than relying on one symptom alone.
Assess severity promptly with vital signs, oxygenation, and a validated pneumonia severity tool.
Management should follow local pathways and account for patient-specific comorbidity and clinical severity.
diagnostic_clues: Chief complaint: sudden severe shortness of breath, chest pain, and fever 3 days after returning from Nigeria

Key HPI features: Presents to emergency department with a 24-hour history of rapidly worsening shortness of breath, sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain, high fever (38.8°C), and productive cough producing rusty-coloured sputum. Three days ago, she returned from a 3-week trip visiting family in rural Nigeria, where she stayed in crowded housing. Complains of chills, rigors, severe fatigue, and feeling completely washed out. Has a history of type 2 diabetes and takes metformin.
Objective/examination findings: Perform focused examination, vital-sign assessment, and diagnosis-specific investigations.
Relevant background/PMH: type 2 diabetes mellitus x6 years, hypertension
Current medications: metformin 1000mg BD, ramipril 5mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming a mild or atypical presentation rules out Community-Acquired Pneumonia.
Relying on a single normal test result to prematurely exclude serious pathology.
Equating transient symptom improvement with resolution of the underlying condition.
Failing to consider clinically important alternative diagnoses.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before appropriate assessment.
Starting treatment without considering contraindications, interactions, or organ function.
Ignoring critical warning signs: Severe hypoxaemia.
management_principles: Assess severity promptly with vital signs, oxygenation, and a validated pneumonia severity tool.
Obtain chest imaging and microbiology where indicated; start empiric antibiotics according to local CAP guidance.
Escalate urgently for hypoxaemia, shock, confusion, or increasing work of breathing.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 48F diabetic with recent travel to Nigeria presents with acute 24-hour fever, rigors, pleuritic right chest pain, rusty sputum, and acute tachypnoea.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: fever 38.9°C, tachypnoea RR 26, HR 110, BP 105/65 mmHg, O2 sat 91% on room air. Chest examination: right lower zone demonstrates classical signs of pulmonary consolidation -> reduced chest expansion on right, dullness to percussion over right base, increased tactile vocal fremitus, bronchial breath sounds (high-pitched, hollow breath sounds with expiration = inspiration), and coarse late-inspiratory crackles. Calculate CURB-65 Pneumonia Severity Score: Confusion (No - 0 points) + Urea >7 mmol/L (Yes, 8.2 mmol/L - 1 point) + Respiratory Rate >=30 (No, 26 - 0 points) + Blood pressure systolic <90 or diastolic <=60 (No, 105/65 - 0 points) + Age >=65 (No, 48 - 0 points) -> Total CURB-65 Score = 1 point (Moderate Risk / Hospital-managed or supervised outpatient; however, given hypoxaemia O2 sat 91% and diabetes, requires urgent hospital admission). Bloods: peripheral blood cultures x2 sets taken before antibiotics, FBC (leukocytosis >18), CRP >150, U&Es (check urea), glucose. Check Urinary Antigen tests for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila. Check Malaria rapid diagnostic antigen test / thick and thin blood films given travel history. Erect Chest X-ray: confirms dense, homogeneous lobar consolidation involving the right lower lobe with visible air bronchograms and blunting of the right costophrenic angle.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP - right lower lobe consolidation, with pneumococcal infection possible). DDx: Pulmonary embolism after recent travel, malaria or another travel-related febrile illness, tuberculosis, and Legionnaires' disease; investigate according to clinical findings and exposure risk.
reference_soap.plan: This presentation needs emergency hospital assessment for hypoxaemia, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, and travel-related infection. Clinicians should monitor vital signs and gas exchange, obtain appropriate cultures, chest imaging, and malaria testing, and provide supplemental oxygen only if indicated to achieve the locally recommended target saturation. After assessment and with local guidance, clinicians may start empiric antimicrobials and give IV fluids if clinically indicated; review treatment when results and clinical response are available.

learning_objectives: Calculate and interpret the CURB-65 pneumonia score while integrating hypoxaemia and diabetic comorbidities to justify hospital admission
Identify classical physical signs of lobar consolidation: dullness to percussion, increased fremitus, and bronchial breath sounds
Explain why empiric antibiotics and supportive treatment require urgent clinician assessment and local-guideline selection
Perform concurrent malaria thick/thin film screening and urinary antigen testing in patients returning from endemic travel

teaching.one_liner: Acute lower respiratory infection with fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, and focal consolidation.
differentials: Malaria or other travel-related febrile illness

must_ask.say: When did the fever start, and have you had shaking chills or rigors with it?

must_ask.objective: Sputum character and pleuritic chest pain
must_ask.say: Is your cough bringing up rusty or coloured sputum, and does the chest pain get worse when you breathe in?
Have you travelled recently, and did you stay anywhere crowded or with poor ventilation?

must_ask.objective: Severity red flags: confusion, hypotension, respiratory rate
must_ask.say: Have you felt confused, very dizzy, or unusually short of breath at rest?
How has your blood sugar been running lately, given your diabetes?

history.answer: I started feeling terribly short of breath and feverish yesterday, and I have this sharp, stabbing pain in the right side of my chest.
It hit me suddenly yesterday, about twenty-four hours ago, and it has become much worse very rapidly.
It is so bad that I am struggling to catch my breath even while resting in bed, and walking to the bathroom makes me feel exhausted.
It has been continuously worsening without any breaks or relief, and I have never had an episode like this before.
Yes, I developed a high fever up to around thirty-nine degrees with violent shaking chills and shivering spells since yesterday.
I have a persistent cough that brings up thick, sticky, rust-colored brownish phlegm.
It is a sharp, stabbing ache on the right side of my lower chest that catches and hurts much worse whenever I breathe in or cough.
No, I haven't heard or felt any whistling or wheezing noises when breathing.
No, I haven't coughed up pure bright red blood, just that rusty-colored brownish phlegm.
Lying flat hurts my chest and makes me feel more breathless, but I haven't woken up gasping at night in the past.
Deep breathing, coughing, and moving around make the chest pain and breathlessness much worse, and nothing seems to help.
My heart feels like it is beating fast because of the high fever and breathlessness, but I haven't fainted or felt like passing out.
No, I feel completely wiped out and weak, but my mind is clear and I am not confused or disoriented.
No, neither of my legs is swollen, red, or painful at all.
I feel totally drained, exhausted, and washed out, like all my strength has vanished.
No, I don't have any tingling or numbness around my hands or lips, and this is definitely not a panic attack.
I just got back three days ago from a three-week trip to visit family in rural Nigeria, where I stayed in crowded housing with many relatives.
I did get bitten by mosquitoes while I was there, and I did not take regular malaria prevention tablets.
Several family members back there had coughs and colds, but no one had known tuberculosis or chronic illnesses that I know of.
I am terrified that I caught tropical malaria or a deadly flu in Africa, and I worry I might collapse and need a breathing machine in intensive care.
I want urgent blood tests for malaria, intravenous fluids, and strong antibiotics right away to fight this pneumonia.
I have had type two diabetes for about six years, and I also have high blood pressure.
I check my blood sugar at home and it usually runs between seven and eight, but I haven't checked it today because I felt so sick.
I have never had any surgeries, and I have never been admitted to a hospital before.
I take metformin one thousand milligrams twice a day for my diabetes, and ramipril five milligrams once a day for blood pressure.
No, I have never had an allergic reaction to any medicines, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products in my life.
I don't drink any alcohol at all.
I work as an administration officer at a local school, and I live at home with my husband.
My mother had diabetes and my father had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of blood clots or chronic lung disease.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my periods are regular, I am not on any hormone pills, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Alert, flushed female appearing acutely unwell in moderate respiratory distress with rapid shallow breathing and intercostal muscle use, with no cyanosis or digital clubbing.
Temperature 38.9°C, blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 91% on room air.
Pink conjunctivae without pallor; sclerae are clear and non-icteric.
Jugular venous pressure is normal and not elevated, measuring approximately 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.
Reduced chest expansion on the right base with increased tactile vocal fremitus over the right lower zone, eliciting sharp pleuritic pain on deep inspiration.
Dullness to percussion over the right lung base; clear resonant percussion note throughout the left lung and upper right fields.
Bronchial breath sounds and coarse late-inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung field; normal vesicular breath sounds without wheezing on the left.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with distinct S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, rubs, or third heart sound.
No peripheral pitting edema in either ankle or lower extremity.
Both calves are symmetrical, soft, and non-tender, with no swelling, warmth, erythema, or palpable cords.
Alert and fully oriented to time, place, and person, with fluent speech and no cognitive clouding or confusion.
